edits.old: A student submitted this sentence to the school paper: Although the stage was crowded the soloist found her spotlight, she sang the final verse the audience fell silent. Two problems are hiding in it: a fused run-on, and a subordinate clause left standing alone. Your job is to rebuild the sentence so it is fully correct — and say which repair rules you used.
edits.new: A student submitted this sentence to the school paper: Although the stage was crowded the soloist found her spotlight, she sang the final verse the audience fell silent. Two problems are hiding in it: a comma splice, and a fused run-on — plus a missing comma after the introductory 'Although' clause if you count a third. Your job is to rebuild the sentence so it is fully correct — and say which repair rules you used.

edits.old: The original hides three problems. 'Although the stage was crowded' is a subordinate-clause fragment standing alone, so it must be attached to a complete sentence with a comma after 'crowded.' 'The soloist found her spotlight, she sang the final verse' is a comma splice: a comma alone cannot join two independent clauses. Fix it by starting a new sentence with a period, or keep it in one sentence with a semicolon or a comma + FANBOYS. Finally, 'the final verse the audience fell silent' is a fused run-on with no punctuation at all, so it needs a period, a semicolon, or a comma plus a FANBOYS conjunction (here 'and' works well).
edits.new: The original hides three problems. 'Although the stage was crowded' is already attached to 'the soloist found her spotlight'; add a comma after 'crowded' to mark the introductory dependent clause. 'The soloist found her spotlight, she sang the final verse' is a comma splice: a comma alone cannot join two independent clauses. Fix it by starting a new sentence with a period, or keep it in one sentence with a semicolon or a comma + FANBOYS. Finally, 'the final verse the audience fell silent' is a fused run-on with no punctuation at all, so it needs a period, a semicolon, or a comma plus a FANBOYS conjunction (here 'and' works well).

edits.old: The comma is the everyday default, but here it creates a comma splice — two independent ideas glued with too weak a mark.
edits.new: The comma is the everyday default, but here it does not properly introduce the explanation of the rule; use a colon. This is not a comma splice because "no trash talking allowed" is not an independent clause.

edits.old: The semicolon feels sophisticated, so it seems like the 'smart' choice. But a semicolon's only job is to join two closely related complete sentences. Here, 'no trash talking allowed' is not a complete sentence, so there is nothing to join — the sentence is introducing an explanation instead.
edits.new: The semicolon feels sophisticated, so it seems like the 'smart' choice. But joining independent clauses is not a semicolon's only use. Semicolons also separate items in a series when the items contain internal commas. Here, 'no trash talking allowed' is not a complete sentence, so there is nothing to join — the sentence is introducing an explanation instead.

edits.old: Got appears three times — it could mean bought, received, found, or reached.
edits.new: Got appears twice in the vague draft. In "got some stuff," it could mean bought, received, or found; in "got a lot done," it means accomplished or completed.

edits.old: All four words could loosely describe checking work twice, but only diligent carries the approving connotation the note needs; lazy, slow, and picky all blame her.
edits.new: Diligent means showing careful, persistent effort, which matches checking every answer twice and carries the approving tone the note needs.

edits.old: A student's first draft says: The speech was really something. Which revised version uses the most precise, audience-appropriate diction? Type the letter of your choice.
edits.new:
A student's first draft says: The speech was really something. Which revised version uses the most precise, audience-appropriate diction for a formal report?
A. The speech was absolutely mind-blowing and unforgettable.
B. The speech was passionate, with long pauses that let key points sink in.
C. The speech was very good and quite interesting.
D. The speech was really something else entirely.

edits.old: Option B names a specific quality (passion) with concrete evidence (the pauses), fitting a formal report; the vague and overwrought options name nothing a reader can check.
edits.new: Option B names a specific quality (passion) with concrete evidence (the pauses), fitting a formal report; the vague and overwrought options name nothing a reader can picture or check.

edits.old: Clean. A dash setting off an abrupt break is standard punctuation, though some guides would prefer parentheses here.
edits.new: Clean. A dash setting off an abrupt break is standard punctuation, though some guides would prefer parentheses here. 'Honestly' at the front is just an informal opener, not a mistake.

edits.old: Clean. A run-on would smash two full sentences together; this one is correctly built. 'Honestly' at the front is just an informal opener, not a mistake.
edits.new: Clean. This sentence is correctly constructed, and the phrase 'in their own words' is appropriately set off with commas.

edits.old: 'She asked for the vote and every student raised a hand and the chair counted them.'
edits.new: 'She asked for the vote every student raised a hand.'

edits.old: The deciding fact is that run-on sentences are grammatical errors under every style guide, while the other options are disputed choices that guides answer differently.
edits.new: This is a fused run-on: the two independent clauses are joined with no punctuation or conjunction, which is a grammatical error under every style guide.

edits.old: 'She asked for the vote and every student raised a hand and the chair counted them.'
edits.new: 'She asked for the vote every student raised a hand.'

edits.old: They are two independent clauses joined by and with no comma
edits.new: She asked for the vote every student raised a hand.

edits.old: Both muy and mucho translate as "very much" or "a lot", so they get swapped.
edits.new: Muy means "very" and is used before adjectives, while mucho means "much" or "a lot" and can also translate as "very much" in phrases like Me gusta mucho. Because the two words can feel interchangeable in English, learners swap them.

edits.old: The pattern is always the same: Name + es + nationality. Es + profession, with no un or una.
edits.new: The pattern is: Name + es + nationality. Es + profession, with no un or una when the profession stands alone: es cantante. When an adjective describes the profession, the indefinite article appears and agrees: es una cantante colombiana.

edits.old: All five chunks are in the right place.
edits.new: All four chunks are in the right place.

edits.old: Only -o adjectives, consonant-ending nationalities and -or adjectives like trabajador change to -a.
edits.new: Many adjectives can form the feminine with -a: adjectives in -o, consonant-ending nationality adjectives, many -or adjectives such as trabajador, and adjectives ending in -án, -ón or -ín. Fácil itself stays the same for both genders.

edits.old: Eighteen is ten and eight: dieci + ocho = dieciocho.
edits.new: Eighteen is ten and eight: dieci + ocho = dieciocho, written as a single word.
